detail.longDescription: - 50k Starship V4 launches a year, each carrying 200 t (20 MW of compute). That’s 137 a day, one every 2 minutes in two windows of roughly 5–7am and 5–7pm local. As Earth spins, the launch site passes under that target orbit twice a day, at local dawn and local dusk. Globally we’re at about 1 launch a day right now. - The always-sunlit orbit needs launches heading north or south over open water. On US coasts only south works, and packing every usable spot with Starship pads gets us to just 25–30 launches a day. We need 5× that. - So we will go out to sea, 300 km off central California. Inside the US EEZ, clear of Cape Mendocino, between the air routes to Hawaii and Asia. Open water both ways gives us both daily windows. - We will place 35 floating pads in one 68 km row, so no rocket flies over another pad. The water is 4 km deep, so thrusters hold the pads in place. - Need a huge daily supply: 190 kt of LNG, 680 kt of liquid oxygen, 27 kt of satellites. - About 7 LNG tankers and 10 liquid-oxygen tankers in constant rotation. - Roughly a container ship a day of satellites from LA, so 2–3 ships in rotation. - About 20 shuttles refilling pads between windows. - The gas for all that is 2.5 times what all of California uses. The California Coastal Commission has really not been playing ball with such things so far. - So we make it in Mexico. Baja’s Costa Azul terminal already turns US pipeline gas into LNG, so we expand that site with much bigger LNG production, a liquid-oxygen plant, new pipeline capacity from Texas to Baja and 20 GW of power. This would be one of the biggest natural gas sites on Earth. Unexplored territory: - Terafab (we need at lesat 0.5M wafer starts per day, mostly memory. This is 10x more than TSMC makes today. maybe doable by 2035) - Starship V4 (scheduled for 2027) catching booster and ship at sea (Falcon boosters already do sea landings with legs) - large liquid-oxygen carriers (essentially an LNG carrier with oxidizer safety) - starship-scale floating pads (Sea Launch did this two decades ago. But much smaller rockets)
